title: The Bookkeeper of the Seventh City
dek: In Chinguetti, Mauritania, a handful of families still guard libraries of Islamic manuscripts older than the town itself. The desert that once made the place rich is now, grain by grain, taking it back.
author: Gemini
body:
The doors are wooden and very old, and when Mohammed Ould Habott opens them the light comes into the room at a low angle and lies flat across the floor. It is close to noon. By afternoon the air outside will climb past forty-three degrees; last night it fell to ten, the way it does in a place with no water to hold the day's heat and no cloud to trap it. The stone walls keep what little cool the dark left behind, which is why the room feels like the inside of a well. Habott is fifty-one. He wears the pale blue of the desert and moves without hurry, because the things on the steel shelves along the wall do not reward hurry. He lifts one down. The cover is leather, wrinkled and darkened the way a hand darkens with age, and the pages inside are the brown of strong tea. He turns them with the tips of his fingers. A diagram of the moon in its phases. An eclipse rendered in faded ink. A drawing of the two holy cities, Mecca and Medina, done by someone who had almost certainly walked to them and back across a thousand kilometers of sand.

"My relationship with them is like that of a father and his son," Habott has said of the manuscripts, and he means it in the full weight of the comparison: the obligation that cannot be refused, the love that does not ask whether it is convenient. He is the eighth man in his family to keep this library, and he did not choose it so much as inherit it, in 2002, when his father grew too sick to lift the books himself. There are roughly fourteen hundred of them here. The oldest was written on paper carried from China in the eleventh century, and it is older than the town outside the door.

That town is Chinguetti, in the Adrar highlands of northern Mauritania, and it is being buried. Not metaphorically. If you walk from Habott's library toward the older quarter, you come after a few hundred meters to houses with sand piled against their walls to the height of a man, then to the height of a window, then to the height of the roof, and then to houses that are simply gone, marked only by a swell in the dune like the shape of something under a blanket. A guesthouse a Belgian built here decades ago stands half-submerged, one story swallowed, the surviving wall the copper color of the dune that leans against it. The Sahara does not besiege Chinguetti in any dramatic sense. It arrives quietly, a few centimeters at a time, on the wind, and it does not leave.

The people who remain, fewer than five thousand of them now, have organized their days partly around this fact. The streets of the old quarter are too narrow for a truck, so when the sand comes in overnight, as it does, men shovel it into panniers and lead mules out through the town to dump it somewhere the town is not. It is the labor of bailing a boat. Melainine Med El Wely, who heads a local association for managing what is left of the oasis, put it to a reporter early last year in the flattest terms available. It is a city, he said, surrounded by an ocean of sand that is advancing every minute.

To understand why the ocean is advancing, and why it was ever held back, you have to hold two clocks at once. One runs in centuries and belongs to the town. The other runs in millennia and belongs to the desert, though lately it has begun to run fast.

Chinguetti keeps its own long time, and it keeps two dates. There was a first settlement, called Abweir, whose ruins lie a little apart and which the town remembers as beginning around the year 777, when the whole apparatus of Saharan trade was still assembling itself. Then there is the town you can walk through now, which local tradition dates to 1264, when Berber tribesmen laid out a fortified settlement at a place where a wadi carried water beneath the surface and date palms could be made to grow. The Arabic word for such a fortified town is *ksar*, plural *ksour*, and Chinguetti became the most important of them. It sat at a hinge in the trans-Saharan trade, the point where the routes running north to the Mediterranean met the routes running south into the empires of gold. The caravans that stopped here were not small. The largest are remembered as thirty thousand camels moving as one body across the sand, and they carried the two commodities that mattered most in that economy, which were not gold and not slaves but salt and paper: salt hacked in slabs from the mines at Idjil to the north, and books, carried in saddlebags, bought and copied and argued over. Gold came up from the Ghana and Mali empires to the south and passed through on its way to the coast. For four centuries, roughly the thirteenth through the seventeenth, this traffic made Chinguetti rich, and the town spent its wealth the way it wanted to be remembered: on scholarship.

It became a place you went to learn. The schools here taught the Quran and the hadith, and also grammar, rhetoric, law, mathematics, astronomy, and medicine, the full apparatus of a medieval university, which is why the town is still often called the Sorbonne of the Sahara. It also became a gathering point for the pilgrimage. Men from across the western desert who could not manage the whole enormous journey to Mecca on their own would assemble at Chinguetti and set out together, so that the town's name became attached to the destination. Over time the pilgrims from this region were known throughout the Muslim world simply as the people of Chinguetti, and Mauritania itself was called Bilad Shinqit, the land of Chinguetti, long before it was called anything else. The town is said, locally, to be the seventh holy city of Islam, a claim you will not find recognized in Cairo or Mecca but which is held here with complete sincerity. At the center of the old quarter stands the Friday Mosque, built of dry stone laid without mortar, its square minaret capped by five finials made from ostrich eggs. It is a national symbol; its image is on the currency. One of the finials, by tradition, points the way to the Kaaba. The minaret is said to be the second-oldest still in continuous use anywhere in the Muslim world, which means that men have been climbing it to call the prayer, without a break, for the better part of the interval between the town's two founding dates.

The manuscripts are the residue of all that learning. They were never a single collection. They accumulated in private houses, family by family, as scholars bought texts in Fez and Cairo and Andalusia, copied them by hand, wrote their own commentaries in the margins, and passed the whole inheritance to a son. Habott's own line runs back to a scholar-collector named Sidi Mohammed Ould Habott; a forebear is said to have traveled as far as Mecca and Muslim Spain to bring texts home. At the height of it, Chinguetti held around thirty of these family libraries and something like six thousand manuscripts. Today thirteen libraries survive, and only about five open their doors to anyone from outside. The rest have gone the way of the houses in the old quarter: closed, dispersed, sold, or simply outlived by their sand.

What is written in them is a cross-section of a civilization's mind. Islamic jurisprudence and Quranic commentary, yes, but also a treatise on the science of poetry, tables of the moon's phases, the mathematics a merchant needed and the astronomy a traveler needed, medical texts, works of Sufism and its interpretation. Some of the pages are illuminated. Many are annotated in several hands across several centuries, one reader answering another across a gap of two hundred years. They are, as Habott says, not only his. "I have to protect this heritage," he told Al Jazeera, "as mine, and also for all of humanity."

Protecting them is a daily physical struggle against the same forces taking the town. The enemies are heat, which dries the paper until it cracks like a dead leaf; humidity, which swings and warps the fibers; sandstorms, which drive grit into any gap; the rare flash flood, which a changing climate has made less rare; and insects. Termites are patient and thorough. To keep the books, one of the Habott family has explained, they took to setting powders in the containers, basins of water, whatever preservative could be got, so the termites would not eat what the heat had not already cracked. In the worst months the keepers put out buckets of water around the room, a homemade humidifier to keep the air from turning the paper to ash. In 2024, UNESCO's Heritage Emergency Fund opened a project with a title that reads like a thesis statement, Connecting Generations Through Safeguarding the Desert Libraries of Mauritania, and put a hundred thousand dollars into thirteen of the town's libraries. The money bought air-conditioning units, steel shelving, and acid-free storage boxes. It is real help and it is a thimble against the sea.

The sea itself has a physics, and the physics is worth understanding, because it explains both how the town was possible and why it is failing.

Sand moves in three ways, and the most important one you can see if you crouch at the edge of a dune on a windy day and watch the surface blur. Grains of a certain size, fine to medium, are light enough for the wind to lift but heavy enough to fall back quickly. The wind picks one up, carries it a short arc, and drops it, and where it lands it strikes other grains and knocks them into arcs of their own, so that the whole surface seems to boil forward in a low, hissing haze about ankle height. This is saltation, from the Latin for leaping, and it does roughly three-quarters of the work of moving a desert. The bouncing grains also shove larger, heavier grains along the ground without ever lifting them, a slow forward roll called creep, which accounts for most of the rest. Almost nothing important happens in the air above the knee. A dune is a machine for turning wind into forward motion, one leap at a time.

Where the wind blows steadily from one direction and the sand supply is limited and the ground beneath is hard, the machine takes a particular and beautiful shape: the barchan, a crescent, its horns pointing downwind. The windward side is a long gentle ramp, ten to fifteen degrees, up which the wind drives the saltating grains toward the crest. At the crest the wind lets go. The grains fall onto the sheltered lee side and pile up there until the slope reaches about thirty-four degrees, the angle of repose, the steepest a heap of dry sand can stand before it fails. Then it fails. A sheet of sand avalanches down the lee face, the slope resets to thirty-four degrees, and the process repeats. Grain by grain the windward side is stripped and the lee side is fed, which means the entire dune crawls forward across the desert in the direction of the wind, its shape preserved even as every grain in it is replaced. Somewhere in the Sahara a barchan advances something like fifteen to twenty meters in a year, though the true figure at any given town is its own local argument between wind and sand.

Now put a house in its path. The dune does not knock the house down. It climbs the windward wall as if the wall were simply more ground, spilling grit through every crack, and when it reaches the top it avalanches down the far side into the courtyard, and it keeps coming, something like fifteen to twenty meters a year, until the roofline is a contour in the sand and the house is inside the dune. This is what happened to the Belgian's guesthouse and to the abandoned rows of the old quarter. The desert is not attacking. It is doing arithmetic.

For most of Chinguetti's history the arithmetic ran the other way, and the reason was water and the things water grows. A dune can migrate only if its grains are free to leap. Vegetation stops them. Roots knit the surface together; stems and leaves break the wind before it can reach the ground and get under a grain; a belt of trees around a town is a wall the sand cannot climb because the sand cannot get moving. Chinguetti sat in an oasis. Acacia and gum trees and, above all, date palms ringed the settlement and drank from a water table close enough to the surface to reach, and their roots and shade held the sand in place and held the dunes at bay. The town was not fighting the desert. It was being sheltered by a living thing the desert could not cross.

That living thing is dying, and the date on its death certificate is the late 1960s.

Beginning around 1968, the whole Sahel, the band of semi-arid country along the desert's southern edge, entered a drought so severe and so prolonged that climate scientists still study it as one of the sharpest regional shifts of the twentieth century. Rainfall across the Sahel fell by more than thirty percent from what it had been in the 1950s, stayed low through the mid-1970s, and struck again in the 1980s. The causes are still argued, with the weight of evidence pointing to a shift in the temperature difference between the northern and southern Atlantic, to industrial aerosols, and later to the broad warming that is now raising temperatures here about one and a half times faster than the global average. The consequences were not argued at all. Crops failed across Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Chad, and Burkina Faso; herds died; something like a hundred thousand people died with them. And the desert, released, moved south.

In Chinguetti the drought worked slowly and then all at once. The rains that recharged the aquifer beneath the oasis thinned to almost nothing. A retired schoolteacher named Mohamed Lemine Bahane, who has kept his own measurements for years, reckons the town has seen about two and a half centimeters of rain a year over the past decade, and by his accounting and others' the region's rainfall has dropped by roughly thirty-five percent since 1970. The water table fell. The wells that had watered the palm groves for seven hundred years began, one after another, to come up dry. And the palms began to die of thirst.

What the drought did not kill, the people finished, not out of carelessness but out of the same need that killed the herds. A family with nothing to burn will cut a dead acacia for firewood. A family with goats and no pasture will strip a living tree for its leaves. The gum trees went, the acacia went, and the palms the falling water table had not already killed were cut for what they could give. Salima Ould Salem, a date farmer of fifty, described her corner of the oasis the way you would describe a house after a funeral. It used to be full of families, she said; they have gradually moved away. Every tree that came down removed a section of the wall that had held the sand still. Every meter the water table dropped killed more of what remained. And once the vegetation was gone the surface was free, the grains could leap, and the barchans that had been idling at the edge of town for centuries did the only thing barchans do. They started to move, toward the houses, at whatever pace the wind allowed.

This is the loop, and it is vicious in the precise sense that each turn tightens the next. Less rain means a lower water table means dying palms means less vegetation means more mobile sand means dunes over the wells and gardens, which buries what water and soil remain, which kills more palms. Nobody in Chinguetti needs the diagram. They live inside it. Habott gave the demography of the loop without any diagram at all. People left, he said, because they wanted to feed themselves, get their kids an education, get a better chance somewhere else. The old quarter emptied house by house the way the library shelves emptied book by book, and for the same underlying reason, which is that it is very hard to keep a fragile inheritance alive in a place the water is leaving.

And yet they stay, some of them, and the staying is not passive. Along the town's windward edge, crews put young trees into the sand and try to raise a green wall to do again what the old oasis did, to break the wind and pin the grains before they can leap. It is the correct idea and it is running uphill: a sapling needs water, and water is the thing that is gone, so the barrier meant to hold back the desert must itself be defended from the desert while it grows. Asked why she does not leave with the others, Salima Ould Salem gave the answer of someone who understands exactly what departure would mean. They prefer to stay, she said. If she left, her place would disappear. She did not mean it would be forgotten. She meant it would be under the sand by the following season, and she is right.

The manuscripts are the sharpest form of the same question, because they are the part of Chinguetti least able to move and least able to be replaced. A person can leave for Nouakchott, the capital on the coast, and many have; the town has been draining toward the city for a generation. A book cannot leave without ceasing to be what it is. Its value is not only in its text, which could in principle be photographed, but in its being here, in this room, in this town, in the unbroken line of a family that has kept it for two hundred years. Habott's ancestor left instructions that read now like a curse and a blessing at once: the library was to stay in Chinguetti, it was to be open to every seeker of knowledge, and it was to be kept by a male descendant who was religious and upright. Habott has honored all three. His two sons, twelve and eighteen, have made him no promises. He suspects they will not take up the duty, and he does not entirely blame them, because he can read the same arithmetic everyone else can.

There have been efforts to save the manuscripts by copying them, digitizing them, moving some to climate-controlled storage in the capital, cataloguing what exists before more of it crumbles. Some of this is real and useful. But it runs into the thing that makes Chinguetti Chinguetti, which is that the town is not a warehouse of documents. It is a place where knowledge was kept in a particular way, by particular families, as a sacred trust rather than a public archive, and to move the books to Nouakchott would preserve the paper while dissolving the thing the paper was part of. Habott is clear-eyed about the stakes and immovable about the response. Protecting the library, he says, is not even a question to be asked. It is a family obligation. His duty, as his ancestor framed it and as he accepts it, does not end when it becomes difficult. It ends only when the town does. They must protect them, he said, until God takes the land and all the people who are on it.

It is worth being precise about what would be lost, because the loss is not abstract. Chinguetti and its three sister *ksour*, Ouadane and Tichitt and Oualata, were inscribed together on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1996 as a single site, the last surviving examples of a kind of place that once threaded the whole Sahara: the caravan towns where a trade in salt and gold and God moved across the largest desert on earth, and where, improbably, in mud and dry stone at the edge of the void, people built universities. That world is already almost entirely gone. The caravans stopped. The routes died when the ships took the gold trade to the coast and the colonial borders cut the desert into countries. What remains of it now is the architecture, the mosque with its ostrich eggs, the manuscripts, and the families who keep them. When those go, the thing does not become endangered. It becomes extinct, the way a language becomes extinct when its last speaker dies, which is to say completely and without appeal.

The town has some time yet. The sand does not move in a season, the people are stubborn, there is a green wall being coaxed out of the ground on the windward edge, and there is a hundred thousand dollars' worth of air-conditioning humming in a few of the libraries against the heat. Chinguetti has been written off before. It was written off when the trade routes died, and it survived as a town of scholars and pilgrims for centuries after the money was gone. It may yet outlast the current forecast, if the rains change, or if the world decides an ancient library at the edge of the Sahara is worth the water it would take to grow a forest around it.

But the arithmetic sits there regardless, patient, doing its work at ankle height. In the cool room with the wooden doors, Mohammed Ould Habott closes the manuscript he has been holding, the one with the moon drawn in its phases and the eclipse and the two holy cities he may never see, and he slides it back into its acid-free box on the steel shelf, and he steps out into the white glare of the afternoon. Behind the town, along the streets too narrow for anything but a mule, the men are leading their animals out again with the panniers full, carrying the night's sand away, one load at a time, to somewhere the town is not yet. The dune they took it from will have it back by morning.

title: The Weight of Paper in a Drowning Town
dek: In Chinguetti, Mauritania, a few families still guard libraries of medieval Islamic manuscripts. Now the Sahara is coming for the last of them.
author: Claude
body:
Every morning, before he opens the library, Mohammed Ould Habott clears the sand from the doorway. It arrives overnight, fine as flour, drifting under the door and pooling on the threshold in a low pale ridge that has to be swept back before anyone can step through. He does it the way other men check the sky. The sand tells him which way the wind blew while he slept, and how hard, and how much closer the desert has come to the room where his family has kept its books for two hundred years.

Inside, the air is cooler and the light is low. Steel shelves line the walls, and on the shelves sit cardboard boxes, and inside the boxes, wrapped and stacked, are roughly fourteen hundred manuscripts. The Qur'an and commentaries on it. The sayings of the Prophet. Treatises on astronomy and mathematics and geometry, works on law and grammar and the measure of poetry, some copied by Habott's own ancestors in a hand that has not been improved on since. The oldest was written on Chinese paper and dates to the eleventh century, which is to say it was already old when the town around it was young. Habott pulls on white cotton gloves before he touches any of it. He lifts a volume, turns the leaves to check for the small brown scars where insects have been at work, and sets it back in its box. He has done this most mornings for more than twenty years.

"My relationship with them is like that of a father and his son," he says of the manuscripts. He took the collection over in 2002, when his own father fell ill, and by the town's count he is the eighth of his line to keep it. He has two boys now, one twelve and one eighteen. Neither has said he wants the job.

This is the arithmetic that governs Chinguetti, and it runs in one direction. The sand is patient and the families are tired. The town sits in the Adrar, a plateau of black rock and ochre gravel in north-central Mauritania, and over the past decade it has taken in, on average, about two and a half centimeters of rain a year. That is not a drought figure. That is the ordinary condition against which droughts are now measured. When the rain does not come, the trees that once held the ground die, and when the trees die the sand moves, and when the sand moves it comes here, to the doorways of the old quarter, where the libraries are.

Melainine Med El Wely, who runs a local association devoted to keeping the oases alive, puts it flatly. "It's a city surrounded by an ocean of sand that's advancing every minute," he says. He is not reaching for a metaphor. He is describing a rate.

To understand what arrives at Habott's door you have to understand how sand travels, because it does not blow in like snow, all at once, in a storm. It walks. When the wind over a desert floor crosses a certain threshold of speed, it lifts the finest grains and throws them forward in low flat arcs. Each grain lands a short distance downwind and strikes the surface like a small hammer, knocking other grains loose and into the air, which land and strike in turn. Geologists call this saltation, from the Latin for leaping, and it accounts for about three-quarters of all the sand a wind moves. The grains too heavy to leap are shoved along the ground by the ones that do, rolling and creeping forward a body-length at a time. A dune is nothing more than the sum of billions of these small forward jumps, a statistical animal made of individual grains that have each, on average, gone a little farther in one direction than any other.

The physics has a cruel economy to it, and it was worked out in the Libyan desert in the 1930s by a British army officer named Ralph Bagnold, who found that the sand a wind carries rises with the cube of its speed. Double the wind and you move eight times the sand. This is why a single afternoon of hard wind can undo a year of stillness, and why the intensifying sandstorms residents describe are not a nuisance but an engine. The grains are always arriving. The storms simply deliver a decade in a day.

Where the wind blows steadily from one quarter, as it does across much of the Sahara, the sand organizes itself into barchans, the crescent dunes that are the desert's most efficient travelers. A barchan has a long gentle back that faces into the wind and a steep curved face on the far side, the slip face, where sand carried up the back spills over and slides down at the angle beyond which dry sand can no longer hold itself, about thirty-four degrees. The horns of the crescent point downwind and run ahead, because the thinner edges of the dune, holding less sand, move faster than the heavy middle. And a barchan does move. The whole crescent marches forward as grains are stripped from the windward back and dropped onto the leeward face, the dune advancing without any single grain making the full journey, the way a wave crosses an ocean while the water stays home. In the open desert these dunes travel between one and thirty meters a year, sometimes more, and the smaller they are the faster they go, because there is less of them to push. A modest dune can cover the length of a house in a single year. It does not care what the house is made of, or what is kept inside.

Chinguetti has watched this happen before, and to a place very like itself. A few kilometers off there was an older settlement, Abweir, and it was abandoned in the thirteenth century, in a year the locals will tell you was 1264, and then quietly swallowed. The sand took it whole. What stands today was raised nearby, on higher and stonier ground, around the same time, and its own name carries the memory of what a desert town runs on. Chinguetti is the Arabic mouthing of Shinqit, and the older Soninke sense of it points to the wells of horses, the water that made a stop in the sand worth stopping at. For a while the choice of ground looked wise.

Because for a few centuries this was one of the crossroads of the medieval world. The Sahara was not an emptiness then but a sea with ports, and Chinguetti was one of the busiest, a mandatory halt for the caravans hauling goods between the Mediterranean and the gold country to the south. Salt came down from the mines in slabs cut like paving stones, so valuable it was traded weight for weight against other goods. Gold came up from the empires of Ghana and Mali. Dates and cloth and copper and enslaved people moved along the same routes, and the camel trains that carried them could run to the thousands, some accounts insisting on figures as high as thirty thousand animals moving as one long river of dust across the plateau. The town grew rich on the traffic, and around the wealth grew something rarer.

It became a place of books. Chinguetti sat at the western edge of the Muslim world, and for the pilgrims of the Maghreb and the Sahel it was the last great gathering point before the long haul east, the place where the faithful massed each year to form the caravans that would carry them to Mecca. They called it the gate to the holy places. In time they called the town itself holy, the seventh city of Islam by a reckoning no council ever ratified but everyone repeated, and the name of the town became the name of the whole country in the mouths of Arabs elsewhere: Bilad Shinqit, the land of Chinguetti, a place known abroad by its scholars before it was known by its borders. Along a lane the residents still call the Rue des Savants, the street of the scholars, men argued jurisprudence and taught rhetoric and law, astronomy and mathematics and medicine, and they copied books, and bought them from the passing caravans, and wrote their own. The libraries that survive are the sediment left by all that talk.

This was the Sahara that produced the Almoravids, the Sanhaja Berber confederation of the western desert whose religious warriors erupted out of these sands in the eleventh century behind a preacher named Abdallah ibn Yasin and went on to rule an empire that reached from the Senegal River to the middle of Spain. The men who built Chinguetti's scholarly tradition were the heirs of that world, a desert Islam that was austere, literate, and mobile, carried on camelback and kept in trunks. When the trunks stopped moving, the books stayed. Something like thirty libraries once operated in the old town, holding among them an estimated six thousand manuscripts. Now the count of the ones still functioning runs somewhere between a handful and a dozen, depending on who is counting and what they mean by open. Almost all are private, the property of the families descended from the merchant-scholars who assembled them, passed down through the generations like the houses themselves, and increasingly with the same problem: fewer people left to hold them up.

Habott's library was built by an ancestor who traveled the width of the Muslim world in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and carried books home. Down the way are other collections, each a room or a few rooms in a family compound of dry stone, each holding things that ought to sit behind glass in a national museum with its own climate plant and are instead in cardboard on a shelf, defended by one man with a set of keys and a duty he did not choose.

The things themselves are extraordinary. In one collection there is a treatise on astronomy, a hundred and thirty-two pages of Arab celestial science bound in leather worn soft as cloth, its diagrams of lunar phases and eclipses drawn by a hand that has been dust for five hundred years, and it lives in a box in a stone house at the edge of a town the maps are starting to forget. There are Qur'ans whose margins bloom with commentary in three directions. There are pages the families say carry the medicine of Ibn Sina, the physician the West called Avicenna, copied and recopied along the caravan routes until they washed up here at the far shore of the paper world. The manuscripts are the reason the four ancient towns of the Adrar, Chinguetti with its sisters Ouadane, Tichitt, and Oualata, were together inscribed as a single UNESCO World Heritage site in 1996, recognized as the surviving remains of a civilization that ran on camels and ink. The listing, in the flat language of committees, records that the towns survive with difficulty, chiefly against the advance of the desert sands. That was thirty years ago. The sands did not pause to read it.

What changed, and why the town that outlived Abweir now finds itself losing the same slow war, begins in the late 1960s, when the rains across the whole width of the Sahel began to fail. From around 1968 through 1973, and again in the early and middle 1980s, the belt of semi-arid land along the desert's southern edge suffered one of the most severe sustained droughts recorded anywhere in the twentieth century. The mechanism was oceanic, a shift in the temperature contrast between the northern and southern Atlantic that starved the region of the summer rains it lived on, and the human cost was enormous. At least a hundred thousand people died across the Sahel between the late 1960s and the early 1980s, some estimates run far higher, and the desert's southern edge lurched down across land that had held grass and herds within living memory. In Chinguetti, already sitting at the desert's dry heart rather than its margin, the drought did not announce itself with famine so much as with a subtraction that never reversed. The rain that used to come simply came less. By one measure Mauritania's rainfall has fallen by more than a third since 1970, and the country is now warming at roughly one and a half times the global rate. Ninety percent of it is desert. The World Bank puts its arable land at under half a percent.

For a desert town this is not weather. It is structural collapse in slow motion, because the town was never fighting the sand on its own. It had allies, and they were green. An oasis is a machine for holding ground: the date palms and the acacia and the gum trees put down roots that fix the soil, and their canopies break the wind before it can lift a grain, and the whole living apparatus depends on water within reach of a root. When the water table falls and the rain does not recharge it, the trees at the margin die first, and where a tree dies a gap opens in the windbreak, and through the gap the sand walks in. Then the process feeds itself. With the acacias buried and the pasture gone, herders have taken to cutting down the date palms, the town's own oasis, to feed the leaves to their starving animals, so that the trees that anchored the ground are fed to the animals that stripped it. Overgrazing and firewood-cutting finish what the drought begins. Every green thing removed is a door held open for the desert.

Salima Ould Salem knows the shape of this by heart. She is fifty, a date farmer, and she now pipes water in from tanks and prunes her trees hard so the little she has is not wasted on branches the tree cannot afford. Her neighborhood used to be full of families. Most are gone now, moved to the cement houses on the modern side of town or out of Chinguetti altogether, and she understands exactly what their leaving means, because a lived-in house is itself a windbreak and an emptied one is a dune waiting to happen. "We prefer to stay here," she says. "If I leave, my place will disappear." She is not speaking figuratively. She has seen the houses of the people who left, and she has seen what comes through their doors.

You can walk the old town and read its losing position in the buildings. The oldest core is simply gone, under the sand, mapped only in memory. Along the current edge the dunes stand at the height of a windowsill and pour into the rooms behind. A guesthouse a Belgian investor put up for the tourists who used to come sits half-drowned, one story of it above the surface and the rest below, a building turned into a measuring stick for the desert. Sand blocks doorways. It fills courtyards. It arrives in the night and has to be swept at dawn, every dawn, from every threshold, an unpaid tax the remaining families pay in the only currency the desert takes, which is attention, and which is running short because the people are running short. The town holds perhaps forty-eight hundred residents now, and the electricity that reaches them steadied only in 2013. For most of the modern history of a place the Arab world once knew by its scholars, the grid flickered.

A retired schoolteacher named Mohamed Lemine Bahane has turned the disappearance into data. He measures the sand where it falls and records the rain when it comes, keeping the kind of long private ledger towns rely on when governments are far away, and he has become an evangelist for the one thing that might actually work, which is trees. Plant enough of them, in the right belt, in the right species, and you rebuild the windbreak the drought tore down. It is the logic behind the Great Green Wall, the pan-African plan to lay a band of vegetation across the whole southern Sahara, and it is sound. It is also brutally hard to run here, because a sapling needs water to survive, and it can take years for a taproot to reach deep enough to drink on its own, and water is exactly the thing the town no longer has to spare. The Ministry of Environment has floated tree projects. European NGOs have floated tree projects. Trees have gone into the ground. There is little sign, so far, that the desert has noticed.

At King's College London, an earth scientist named Andreas Baas studies how the winds and dunes of places like this shift as the climate warms, the changing patterns that decide which way the sand will walk and how fast. His finding does not comfort. In a 2022 paper with a colleague, Baas modeled the world's dune fields under warming and concluded that in the tropical and equatorial belts, the ones that hold Chinguetti, dunes are likely to migrate faster by the end of the century, and to swing direction as the prevailing winds reorganize. A town has some defense against a sand that always comes from the same quarter. It has almost none against a sand that changes its mind. And it is the standing irony of the science that the more precisely researchers can map the advance, the plainer it becomes how little precision alone can stop it. You can know the migration rate of a barchan to within a meter and still have no way to tell it no.

What can be done, people are trying to do, page by page rather than dune by dune. In 2024 UNESCO put a hundred thousand dollars from its emergency heritage fund toward thirteen of the family libraries, money for boxes and shelving and training, the unglamorous hardware of survival. The families do what they have always done, which is more intimate and more desperate. Against the termites and the beetles that tunnel through the paper they set out powders and shallow basins of water. Against the heat, which now regularly pushes past forty-three degrees in the afternoon before the desert night drops it to ten, they keep the manuscripts deep in the coolest rooms, in the cardboard and the cotton and the dark. It is preservation performed with the tools of a household against forces sized for a continent. Habott inspects his fourteen hundred books one at a time, looks for the damage, wraps them again, and puts them back on the steel.

The deeper threat is not the sand at the door or the beetle in the binding. It is that the chain of keepers is coming to its last link. For as long as anyone can name, the manuscripts survived because there was always someone whose whole identity was bound up in keeping them, a son raised to the duty from childhood, fluent in the classical Arabic the books are written in, tied by blood to the room. That world is ending in a single generation. The young people are leaving for Atar and Nouakchott and beyond, for electricity that does not blink, for work, for water that comes from a tap, and who can blame them. A manuscript is a heavy inheritance in a town the desert is closing over. Habott knows the shape of what is coming better than anyone, and he has made his peace with the part he can control and prays about the part he cannot. He will keep the books as long as he is there to keep them. What he asks for is time, and lineage, and in his mouth the two words mean the same thing.

"An ocean of sand is coming," he says. "I ask Allah to keep this family going."

Outside his door the wind has been working all afternoon, and the dune at the end of the lane has moved again, the length of a hand, maybe more, its horns reaching a little farther toward the mosque with its square minaret and the five ostrich eggs set at its corners, the oldest standing thing in a town built to outlast the desert and slowly failing to. Tonight the sand will come under the door and pool on the threshold, fine and pale, the way it has every night for longer than anyone can remember. In the morning Habott will pick up the broom and sweep it back, and open the boxes, and begin.
